To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the downsampling within the moving average coarse-graining procedure is not required to quantify the multiscale entropy of short signals.

the use of a low-pass filter with no downsampling is the optimal approach to estimate multiscale entropy for short time series, whereas the classical coarse-grained multiscale entropy approach, with or without downsampling, is the optimal approach for long time series.

1) the use of downsampling in the coarse-graining process may not be necessary for short signals, and may be detrimental to the estimation of complexity in long signals; 2) the refine composite method may be more appropriate for long signals and relatively high levels of noise; 3) the choice between the moving average and Butterworth filters depends on the sampling frequency and the level of noise in the signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a multiscale entropy approach for univariate signals, which is robust to noise and suitable for short recordings.
the development of a multiscale entropy approach that can be used to analyze short and noisy signals.
the development of a new methodology for the estimation of the complexity of univariate signals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the choice of the filtering method depends on the specific application and the type of signals to be analysed.
the use of downsampling in coarse-graining is a matter of convenience and the choice of the best method depends on the specific needs of each case.
the classical coarse-grain approach with downsampling is the best choice for the evaluation of multiscale sample entropy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, when dealing long signals and relatively high levels of noise, downsampling within the classical coarse-grain approach may be required to quantify complexity in short signals.
, when the signal length is not an issue, downsampling is not required to obtain reliable entropy estimations.

the classical coarse-grained approach, which is based on a moving average filter, is a good option for the analysis of short time-series, while for long ones, it is recommended to use the refine composite approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of the filtering method in the coarse-graining step should be carefully selected depending on the specific application at hand, and the downsampling step may not be required in all cases.

the classical multiscale approach is a robust tool to analyze the complexity of long signals, while the refine composite method is a more appropriate choice to analyze the complexity for shorter signals.
downsampling within coarse-graining is not always necessary to quantify the complexity in short signals, especially for those with low sampling frequency.
